dek: VeriFone made the card terminals on store counters, so any shop could take credit and debit cards.
lede: The company that read your card at the checkout counter started in Honolulu, making devices that checked whether a check was good. VeriFone was founded there in 1981. It spent several years inside Hewlett-Packard, then came back out as an independent business backed by private equity. By the spring of 2005, chip cards were spreading across Europe and Asia. Every merchant needed hardware that could keep up with the card networks, and VeriFone wanted to sell it to them.

sections.heading: A Clerk's Phone Call, Replaced
sections.body: The bet was that the moment a customer pays should be fast, cheap and trusted. Early VeriFone devices replaced the phone call a clerk made to check a card. Later models added PIN pads, receipt printers and secure software. VeriFone sold through banks and payment processors as well as directly, so its terminals spread far beyond any one retailer. That installed base was the quiet engine of the business. Every upgrade cycle turned old terminals into new orders.

sections.heading: A Ticker Called PAY
sections.body: VeriFone priced its offering at $10 a share in April 2005 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker PAY. It bought Lipman Electronic Engineering in 2006, then pushed into taxi screens and mobile payments. Newer readers that worked with phones squeezed the old terminal business. In 2018 Francisco Partners took VeriFone private in a deal worth about $3.4 billion.

tagline: Chicago's Options Pit, in a Browser
dek: optionsXpress let everyday investors trade stock options online for low fees, with tools once kept for professionals.
lede: Options trading once belonged to the floor traders packed into Chicago's pits. optionsXpress, founded in that city in 2000, put the same contracts in front of ordinary investors through a web browser. It gave them pricing and strategy tools that had been rare outside professional desks. The company went public in January 2005. Online brokers were climbing back from the dot-com crash, and a new wave of active traders wanted cheaper, faster ways to trade.

sections.heading: Built Around Options
sections.body: The founders bet that retail investors would trade options if someone made it easy and cheap. Most brokers treated options as an add-on to stock trading. optionsXpress built its whole platform around them, with option chains, calculators and lessons for self-directed traders. Low flat commissions drew active customers, and the firm earned well on each account. It stayed lean and profitable, which set it apart from many brokers of its era.

sections.heading: Folded Into Schwab
sections.body: optionsXpress priced its IPO at $16.50 a share in January 2005 and traded on Nasdaq as OXPS. It stayed profitable in the years that followed. It added futures trading and bought other brokerage businesses. In 2011 Charles Schwab acquired optionsXpress in a stock deal worth about $1 billion. Its options tools and its active-trader customers became part of one of the largest brokers in the United States.

cover.artwork: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare

tagline: A Stock Exchange for Phone Minutes
dek: Arbinet let phone carriers buy and sell routes for international calls on one exchange, without private deals.
lede: Every international phone call passes from one carrier to another, and in the 1990s those handoffs ran on slow, private deals. Arbinet turned that market into an exchange. Carriers posted the routes they could offer and the prices they would pay. Arbinet matched them, routed the traffic and settled the bills. It went public in December 2004, as voice-over-IP cut the cost of calls and carriers hunted for cheap routes.

sections.heading: Minutes as a Commodity
sections.body: Arbinet treated phone minutes like any other commodity. Its platform let a small carrier in one country reach buyers it would never meet in person. Arbinet took on the credit risk and the settlement, and it earned a fee on each minute traded. The model worked best when many small, nimble carriers wanted global routes. They could trade on one exchange instead of signing dozens of separate contracts.

sections.heading: Thin Margins, Long Lines
sections.body: Arbinet priced its shares at $17.50 in December 2004, above the range it first set, and listed on Nasdaq as ARBX. Volume on the exchange grew. The price of each minute kept falling as calls moved to the internet and to mobile phones. Arbinet spent the next years adding services and cutting costs. In 2011 Primus Telecommunications acquired the company, and Arbinet's run as a public company ended.

fate: Renamed Market Leader; acquired by Trulia, 2013 ($355M)
tagline: Your Home's Value, Sold to Agents
dek: HouseValues told homeowners what their houses were worth for free, then sold their names to local agents.
lede: HouseValues traded on Nasdaq under the ticker SOLD, and the ticker fit the business. Near the top of the American housing boom, homeowners wanted to know what their houses might fetch. The Seattle-area company let them type in an address online. A local agent then followed up with a market report, and agents paid HouseValues for each contact. It went public in December 2004, in a market that seemed like it would only go up.

sections.heading: A Curious Homeowner, Sold
sections.body: HouseValues bet that the internet could fill an agent's pipeline better than mailers or open houses. A homeowner checking a price was an early sign of a future listing. The company sold those signals to agents by territory, on subscription. As it grew, it added buyer leads and tools for agents to manage their contacts. Its fortunes rose and fell with the number of agents who were busy and willing to spend.

sections.heading: When Housing Turned
sections.body: The company priced its IPO at $15 a share in December 2004 and listed on Nasdaq. When the housing market turned in 2006 and 2007, agents cut spending and revenue fell with them. HouseValues rebuilt itself as a software company for agents and renamed itself Market Leader. In 2013 Trulia bought Market Leader for about $355 million. Zillow later acquired Trulia.

cover.theme: an old farmhouse (what is my home worth)

dek: Ninetowns let Chinese exporters and importers file inspection and quarantine forms online instead of on paper.
lede: Every container leaving a Chinese port needed inspection and quarantine paperwork, and companies carried stacks of it to a government office. Ninetowns, based in Beijing, built software that let them file those forms online with the agency in charge. China was becoming the workshop of the world, and the filings kept multiplying. Ninetowns offered its American depositary shares in December 2004, when investors were eager for a piece of China's internet and software market.

sections.heading: In the Path of Filings
sections.body: Ninetowns bet that as China's trade boomed, the state would move customs and inspection work onto computers. It built the software that companies used to talk to the inspection system. That put Ninetowns in the path of a large and growing flow of filings. Its customers were thousands of exporters who needed the tools to keep their goods moving through the ports.

sections.heading: A Buyout at $1.80
sections.body: Ninetowns priced its ADSs at $11 in December 2004 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker NINE. Its core business slowed, and the company tried new ventures. The stock fell far below its offering price. In 2012 a group of directors and officers led by chief executive Wang Shuang proposed to buy out the public shareholders. The deal closed in 2014 at $1.80 per share.

cover.theme: boats pulling oars under autumn skies (a trading nation)
cover.artwork: Pulling Oars under Clearing Autumn Skies 晴秋涉櫂圖

dek: InPhonic let shoppers compare cell phones and plans online, often with the phone thrown in free.
lede: InPhonic handed out cell phones for free or nearly free, and the carriers covered the cost. Shoppers on its websites picked a phone and a plan side by side. Each carrier paid InPhonic a commission for every new customer it signed. Americans were trading up to camera phones and comparing plans from a crowded field of carriers. The Washington, D.C. company went public in November 2004, as people got used to buying big things online.

sections.heading: Commissions Pay for Handsets
sections.body: InPhonic bet that buying a phone plan, a confusing purchase full of fine print, would move online. It ran its own sites and powered stores for other brands. Carrier commissions paid for the cheap handsets. The model grew fast, and its sites became some of the largest online sellers of wireless plans in the country. It also rested on two weak points: rebates, and customers staying with their carriers long enough for the commissions to hold.

sections.heading: Rebates and Reckoning
sections.body: InPhonic priced its IPO at $19 a share in November 2004, above its first range of $15 to $17, and listed on Nasdaq. Revenue grew quickly, and losses grew too. Customers complained about slow and missing rebates. Carriers clawed back their payments when subscribers cancelled early. In November 2007 InPhonic filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, and a new owner bought its assets soon after.

cover.theme: telegraphic love (a phone in the mail)

dek: MarketAxess let big investors trade corporate bonds on a screen, asking many dealers for prices at once.
lede: A big investor buying corporate bonds in 2004 still picked up the phone and called dealers one at a time. Stocks had already moved onto screens. MarketAxess, founded in New York in 2000, let those investors ask many dealers for prices at once and trade electronically. When it went public in November 2004, it was one of the few survivors from a crowded field of bond-trading startups born in the dot-com years.

sections.heading: Many Dealers, One Request
sections.body: MarketAxess bet that corporate bonds would follow stocks onto electronic markets. Bonds trade less often than stocks and come in far more varieties, which made that a harder bet. MarketAxess began by letting investors request quotes from several dealers in one step. That saved time and got better prices. Over time it let investors trade with each other, and it built data products from the trades flowing through its system.

sections.heading: Twenty Years as MKTX
sections.body: MarketAxess priced its shares at $11 in November 2004 and listed on Nasdaq. Electronic bond trading spread a little more each year, and the company grew with it. It added high-yield, emerging-market and international bonds. It became one of the leading venues for credit trading worldwide. More than twenty years after its offering, it is still public and trades as MKTX.

tagline: The First Gay IPO, Ticker LGBT
dek: PlanetOut gave gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people a place online to find news and each other.
lede: PlanetOut was the first gay-focused company to trade its stock on a major exchange, and it picked the ticker LGBT. In the mid-1990s the web offered many gay and lesbian people something new: a private, safe way to find each other. PlanetOut, founded in San Francisco in 1995, became one of the first online homes for that community. It merged with Gay.com and built a business on news, personals and paid memberships. It went public in October 2004.

sections.heading: Personals, News and Members
sections.body: PlanetOut bet that a community mainstream media ignored would gather online, and that advertisers would follow. Its sites mixed news, personals and forums. Paid memberships became an important source of revenue, and the company built a strong base of paying subscribers. PlanetOut saw itself as a media brand for a whole audience. It expanded into print and travel to reach that audience in more places.

sections.heading: The Advocate, Bought and Sold
sections.body: PlanetOut priced its IPO at $9 a share in October 2004 and listed on Nasdaq. In November 2005 it bought LPI Media, the publisher of The Advocate and Out. Growth slowed as social networks and free dating sites drew users away. The print and travel businesses struggled, and the company sold them off. In 2009 PlanetOut combined with Here Media, and its run as an independent public company ended.

tagline: PC Mall's Bargain Bin, Spun Out
dek: eCOST.com sold cheap computers, cameras and closeouts online, in deals that vanished when stock ran out.
lede: eCOST.com went public at $5.80 a share, far below the $9 to $11 range it first set. The web store began inside PC Mall, a catalog seller of computers and gear, and was spun out as its own public company in August 2004. Its pitch was bargains: refurbished laptops, closeout cameras and daily deals that disappeared when stock ran out. Online electronics shopping was growing fast, and margins were famously thin.

sections.heading: Deals That Disappear
sections.body: eCOST bet that price-hunting shoppers would come back again and again for short-lived deals. It used the buying power and warehouse of its former parent to offer a wide range of tech products at low prices. Free shipping offers and email deals kept customers returning. The trouble was the crowd of rivals. A bargain market rewards whoever is willing to earn the least on each sale.

sections.heading: Passed From Owner to Owner
sections.body: eCOST listed on Nasdaq in August 2004 under the ticker ECST. Sales grew, then losses followed and the stock fell. In February 2006 PFSweb, an e-commerce services company, completed a stock merger with eCOST. PFSweb sold the eCOST assets back to PC Mall in 2011 for $2.3 million. The brand changed hands again after that, while larger rivals such as Amazon and Newegg took over the market.

cover.theme: a warehouse on the wharf (bargains by the pallet)

dek: RightNow let companies answer customer questions by web, email and phone, with software rented over the internet.
lede: RightNow sold software over the internet from Bozeman, Montana, a long way from Silicon Valley. Greg Gianforte started the company in 1997 so businesses could handle customer questions online. Customers rented the software by subscription and never installed it, years before that became the standard way to buy business software. When RightNow filed to go public in the summer of 2004, many investors still doubted that renting software over the internet could work.

sections.heading: Answers Without a Phone Call
sections.body: RightNow bet that companies would rather rent customer-service software than install it themselves. Its first product was a searchable knowledge base that let customers find answers without calling. It then added email handling, call-center tools and feedback surveys. From its office in the mountains it signed up government agencies and big consumer brands. Its success turned Bozeman into a small hub for software work.

sections.heading: From Bozeman to Redwood
sections.body: RightNow priced its IPO at $7 a share in August 2004 and listed on Nasdaq. The timing proved good for a company that rented its software. Software-as-a-service took off over the following years, and RightNow's revenue grew steadily. It became one of the better-known names in customer-service software. Oracle agreed to buy RightNow in 2011 for about $1.5 billion and closed the deal in early 2012.

cover.theme: a boy holding an hourglass (right now)
cover.artwork: Boy Holding Hourglass and Chinese Fan

dek: Greenfield Online let brands and researchers survey the right people online in days instead of weeks.
lede: Microsoft paid about $486 million for a survey company, and what it wanted most was a European shopping site. Greenfield Online, based in Wilton, Connecticut, started by moving market research onto the internet. It built large panels of people who agreed to answer questions online, and research firms and brands paid for the answers. Market research had long meant phone calls during dinner and clipboards in malls. Greenfield went public in July 2004.

sections.heading: Panels Replace Phone Banks
sections.body: Greenfield bet that the internet would make surveys faster and cheaper than any phone bank. A large online panel, with known details about each member, let researchers reach the right people in days instead of weeks. Online panels became the standard tool of market research in the years that followed. In April 2005 Greenfield bought Ciao, a European site where shoppers compared prices and wrote reviews. Ciao brought shopping referrals and its own survey community.

sections.heading: The Ciao Prize
sections.body: Greenfield Online priced its IPO at $13 a share in July 2004 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker SRVY. Ciao grew into a major part of the company. In 2008 Microsoft agreed to buy Greenfield for about $486 million, mainly to add Ciao to its search and shopping efforts in Europe. Microsoft later sold the survey business to Toluna for $40 million.

fate: Taken private by Bain Capital and partners, 2017 ($500M)
tagline: Engagement Rings Bought on a Screen
dek: Blue Nile let people shop for diamonds online, with grades and prices in the open, for less.
lede: Few people expected anyone to buy an engagement ring online. Diamonds were costly, emotional purchases sold in hushed stores with heavy markups. Blue Nile, founded in Seattle in 1999, put thousands of certified diamonds on the web with their cut, color, clarity and carat in plain view. By the time it went public in May 2004, it had shown that careful buyers would spend thousands of dollars on a ring they had only seen on a screen.

sections.heading: Grading Reports Beat Velvet
sections.body: Blue Nile bet that information would beat atmosphere. It listed grading reports and prices openly, so shoppers could compare stones the way they compared other goods. Suppliers held most of the diamonds Blue Nile listed. That kept its costs low and let it charge far less than a typical store. Its return policy and certified grading gave buyers the confidence to spend.

sections.heading: From Website to Showroom
sections.body: Blue Nile priced its IPO at $20.50 a share in May 2004 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker NILE. The stock rose sharply on its first day. Blue Nile became the best-known online jeweler in America and expanded abroad. In 2017 a group led by Bain Capital took the company private for about $500 million. After that, the online jeweler opened physical showrooms.

cover.theme: the Jewel River of Plovers (jewels and water)
cover.artwork: The Jewel River of Plovers (Chidori no Tamagawa), from an untitled series of Six Jewel Rivers

dek: TOM Online sold ringtones, games and text alerts to Chinese mobile phone users, billed through their carrier.
lede: TOM Online ran a Chinese web portal, and most of its money came from ringtones. It also sold pictures, games and text message alerts to phone users through China Mobile. Early in 2004 China had more mobile phones than any other country. TOM Online was part of TOM Group, a Hong Kong conglomerate. It listed in New York and Hong Kong in March 2004, in the middle of a rush of Chinese internet offerings.

sections.heading: Small Fees, Over and Over
sections.body: TOM Online bet that Chinese users would pay small amounts, over and over, for content on their phones. The carriers collected the fees and passed a share back. The model could grow quickly. It also rested on rules the carriers set, and the carriers could change their billing policies with little warning. Many Chinese internet companies of that era depended on the same kind of mobile revenue.

sections.heading: China Mobile Changes the Rules
sections.body: TOM Online priced its shares at about $15.55 per ADS in March 2004, the top of its expected range. It traded on Nasdaq as TOMO and on the Hong Kong exchange. Changes in China Mobile's billing rules hit the wireless business hard over the next few years. In 2007 the parent company, TOM Group, bought out the minority shareholders and took TOM Online private.

tagline: Flowers Shipped Straight From the Farm
dek: ProFlowers shipped fresh flowers in a box straight from the grower, skipping the local florist.
lede: A bouquet sent across the country used to sit in coolers for days, passing through a wire service and a local florist before it reached the door. Jared Polis, a young internet entrepreneur, founded ProFlowers in 1998 to skip all that. Customers ordered online, and the stems shipped in a box straight from the farm. By the time its parent, Provide Commerce, went public in December 2003, ProFlowers was one of the largest flower sellers online.

sections.heading: No Florist, No Warehouse
sections.body: The bet was that cutting out the middle of the supply chain would mean fresher flowers and lower prices. ProFlowers carried almost no inventory. Growers packed and shipped each order, and Provide Commerce's software coordinated the work. The company later applied the same model to gourmet foods and fruit, and it bought rival gift sellers. Demand came in steep seasonal peaks. The software had to handle a few huge days each year.

sections.heading: Valentine's Day at Scale
sections.body: Provide Commerce priced its IPO at $15 a share in December 2003 and listed on Nasdaq. Sales grew around big gift holidays such as Valentine's Day and Mother's Day, and the company kept buying other businesses. In 2006 Liberty Media bought Provide Commerce for about $477 million. Jared Polis left the business world for a career in politics. The ProFlowers brand continued under later owners for many years.

fate: Taken private by Carlyle and Providence, 2007; later acquired by Fiserv, 2013
tagline: The Engine Room of Small Banks
dek: Open Solutions gave community banks and credit unions modern software to run their accounts and transactions.
lede: Open Solutions priced its IPO at $17 a share, above the $14 to $16 range it had set. The Glastonbury, Connecticut company sold core systems: the software that tracks a bank's deposits, loans and every transaction. Large banks built their own or bought from a few giant vendors. Open Solutions served community banks and credit unions, with modern software built on open, standard databases. It went public in November 2003, as smaller banks replaced aging systems to compete online.

sections.heading: One Database for Small Banks
sections.body: Open Solutions bet that smaller banks wanted the same flexible, modern technology as the giants. Its core platform used a single shared database. That made it easier for a bank to add new products and connect other software. The company grew by winning new banks and by buying other vendors in the same market. Customers tended to stay for years, since replacing a bank's core system is slow and risky.

sections.heading: Carlyle, Then Fiserv
sections.body: Open Solutions listed on Nasdaq under the ticker OPEN in November 2003. It kept buying smaller companies to widen its offering. In 2007 the private equity firms Carlyle Group and Providence Equity Partners took it private in a deal valued at about $1.4 billion. Fiserv, one of the largest providers of bank technology, acquired Open Solutions in 2013. Its software kept running inside many small banks and credit unions.

cover.artwork: Young Woman at an Open Half-Door

fate: Bankrupt, 2008; brand sold to Provide Commerce
tagline: The Gift in the Red Box
dek: RedEnvelope picked upscale gifts for busy shoppers and shipped them wrapped in its signature red box.
lede: RedEnvelope wanted to do the choosing for you. The online gift shop picked the presents, wrapped them and shipped them in its signature red box. It built a brand on that packaging and on a hand-picked selection. When it went public in September 2003, e-commerce offerings were rare and investors were cautious. RedEnvelope was one of the few online retailers willing to test the market after the crash. It sold its shares through a Dutch auction.

sections.heading: Gifts for the Busy Shopper
sections.body: RedEnvelope bet that busy shoppers would pay for a well-edited gift and a strong brand. It sold engraved keepsakes, home goods and holiday items, many of them exclusive. Catalogs drove much of its traffic. Free gift wrapping and personalized items set it apart from larger stores. The business was heavily seasonal. A large share of each year's sales landed in the weeks before Christmas.

sections.heading: The Last Delivery
sections.body: RedEnvelope priced its IPO at $14 a share in September 2003 and listed on Nasdaq as REDE. High marketing and shipping costs kept a steady profit out of reach. In 2008 the company filed for bankruptcy. Provide Commerce, the parent of ProFlowers, bought the RedEnvelope brand and assets. The name lived on as a gift brand under its new owner, sold alongside flowers and other gifts.

cover.theme: a decorated envelope with hibiscus (a gift)

dek: iPass gave business travelers one account to get online anywhere, by dial-up, hotel network or Wi-Fi.
lede: Before smartphones and free Wi-Fi, a business traveler's laptop was only as useful as the next phone jack. iPass struck deals with hundreds of internet providers to build a global network of access points. It sold companies one account that worked almost anywhere. Its software found a local connection and handled the billing behind the scenes. iPass went public in July 2003, one of the first tech offerings to do well after the crash.

sections.heading: Other People's Networks
sections.body: iPass bet that it could stitch other companies' networks into one service and sell it to corporate IT departments. It owned little infrastructure of its own. Its value lay in the agreements, the client software and the security that made remote access safe for large employers. As travelers moved from dial-up to hotel broadband and Wi-Fi, iPass followed them. Large corporations signed on to give their whole traveling workforce one way to connect.

sections.heading: A Long Way From Dial-Up
sections.body: iPass priced its IPO at $14 a share in July 2003 and listed on Nasdaq. The shares rose sharply at first. Over the next decade, free Wi-Fi and mobile data wore away the need for its service. The company shifted toward Wi-Fi software and data. Pareteum, a telecom software company, acquired iPass in early 2019. By then its original dial-up service was long gone.

cover.artwork: Nissaka: Sayo Mountain Pass (Nissaka, Sayo no nakayama), from the series "Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido (Tokaido gojusan tsugi no uchi)," also known as the Hoeido Tokaido

dek: Plumtree gave each employee one web page that pulled together the company's applications and documents.
lede: Plumtree took the idea behind My Yahoo and brought it inside the company firewall. Office workers had to hunt across dozens of systems for the information they needed. Plumtree, founded in San Francisco, gave each employee a single web page built from small windows called portlets. Each portlet drew data from a different source. Plumtree went public in June 2002, after it cut its expected price range from $13 to $15 down to $7 to $9.

sections.heading: One Front Door
sections.body: Plumtree bet that companies would want one front door to all their software. Its portal pulled in content from many vendors, so large organizations with mixed systems found it useful. Big customers, including government agencies, adopted it widely. The portal often became the internal home page that thousands of employees saw each morning. Co-founder Glenn Kelman later became the chief executive of Redfin.

sections.heading: Bought by BEA
sections.body: Plumtree priced its IPO at $8.50 a share in June 2002 and listed on Nasdaq. It was one of the few software companies to go public that year, and it grew modestly as the economy recovered. Larger vendors began bundling portals with their own platforms. In 2005 BEA Systems acquired Plumtree for about $200 million and folded it into its own portal products. Oracle later bought BEA.

fate: Still public as Beyond, Inc. (NYSE: BYON)
dek: Overstock.com sold other companies' surplus goods online at deep discounts, then moved into furniture and home goods.
lede: When the dot-com crash left warehouses full of unsold goods, Overstock.com was ready to buy them. Patrick Byrne founded the company in Salt Lake City in 1999. It sold excess inventory from other retailers and manufacturers at deep discounts. Overstock went public in May 2002 through a Dutch auction, an unusual way to sell shares. By then it was one of the better-known bargain sites on the web.

sections.heading: Liquidation by Website
sections.body: Overstock bet that the internet was the ideal place to clear surplus stock. Liquidation had always been a messy business of brokers and outlet stores. A single website could reach millions of bargain hunters at once. Its quirky ads and low prices made it a household name. Over time the company shifted from closeouts toward new home furnishings, where it found steadier supply and better margins.

sections.heading: Buying Bed Bath & Beyond
sections.body: Overstock priced its offering at $13 a share in May 2002 and listed on Nasdaq. Its outspoken founder made headlines, with campaigns against short sellers and an early push into blockchain projects. Byrne left in 2019. In 2023 the company bought the Bed Bath & Beyond brand and renamed itself Beyond, Inc. It still trades publicly, on the New York Stock Exchange as BYON.

dek: Netflix mailed DVD rentals with no late fees, then became the world's largest subscription streaming service.
lede: Netflix went public with several hundred thousand subscribers and a stack of red envelopes. Most Americans in 2002 rented movies from a video store and paid late fees when they forgot to return them. Netflix charged a monthly subscription instead. Customers built a queue on the website, and DVDs arrived in the mail. Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph founded the company in 1997. When it went public in May 2002, many investors doubted it could survive against Blockbuster.

sections.heading: A Disc Built for Mail
sections.body: Netflix bet on two things. The first was that the cheap, light DVD could travel by mail. The second was that a subscription with no late fees would keep customers loyal. Its recommendation engine pointed people to older films they had never heard of, which made the large catalog valuable. From the start, the founders talked about one day delivering movies over the internet.

sections.heading: From Mailbox to Stream
sections.body: Netflix priced its IPO at $15 a share in May 2002 and listed on Nasdaq. It began streaming in 2007 and started producing original series in 2013. It expanded to nearly every country in the world. Blockbuster, the rival investors once feared, went bankrupt in 2010. Netflix is still public and trades as NFLX, and it is one of the most valuable media companies on earth.

dek: BAM! Entertainment made video games starring familiar cartoon, movie and sports characters for nearly every console.
lede: BAM! Entertainment went public only weeks after the September 11 attacks, in one of the quietest markets for new offerings in years. Its bankers had once hoped for $12 to $14 a share. It sold at $8. Ray Musci founded the San Jose company in 1999 to publish games for a new generation of machines: the PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube and Game Boy Advance. Many of its games starred well-known licensed characters.

sections.heading: Familiar Faces on Crowded Shelves
sections.body: BAM bet that familiar brands would let a young publisher stand out on crowded store shelves. It signed licenses for cartoon and movie properties and paid outside studios to build the games. That let it release titles quickly. It also meant paying large sums up front for licenses, with no guarantee the games would sell. It released games for nearly every major console and handheld of the period.

sections.heading: Game Over
sections.body: BAM priced its IPO at $8 a share in November 2001 and listed on Nasdaq as BFUN. Several of its games sold poorly, and the cost of licenses and development outran revenue. The company cut staff. It sold its London studio to VIS Entertainment, then later bought VIS. Nasdaq delisted BAM in 2004. It released a few more titles until 2005, when it went out of business after a bankruptcy filing.

cover.artwork: Fireworks at Ryōgoku  (Ryōgoku  hanabi), from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei)

fate: Still public as Bread Financial (NYSE: BFH)
tagline: Air Miles and Store Credit Cards
dek: Alliance Data ran the store credit cards and rewards programs behind familiar retail brands.
lede: The store credit card in your wallet and the Air Miles in your account could both lead back to Alliance Data. The investment firm Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe assembled the company in 1996. It combined a retail credit card bank with a transaction processing business, then added the Canadian Air Miles program soon after. By June 2001 it was a quiet giant serving millions of shoppers. It went public that month in a weak market, months after the dot-com crash.

sections.heading: Data From Every Swipe
sections.body: Alliance Data bet that retailers would hand their loyalty and credit card programs to a specialist. Store cards and rewards programs produced detailed data about what customers bought. Alliance Data used that data to let retailers market more precisely. It also earned interest and fees on the cards it issued. Later it added the Epsilon marketing business. Its programs reached millions of households through familiar store brands.

sections.heading: Breaking Into Pieces
sections.body: Alliance Data priced its IPO at $12 a share in June 2001 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It grew for years through acquisitions and joined the S&P 500. In 2019 it sold Epsilon to Publicis for $4 billion. In 2021 it spun off its loyalty business, including Air Miles. In 2022 the remaining card business renamed itself Bread Financial, which still trades on the New York Stock Exchange.

cover.artwork: A Study for the Card Players

tagline: Trading Stocks Without a Floor Broker
dek: Instinet let big investors trade stocks directly by computer, privately and even after the exchanges closed.
lede: Instinet was trading stocks on computer terminals in 1969. Big institutions used it to trade with each other directly, without a floor broker. Reuters bought it in 1987. By the late 1990s Instinet and newer rivals were taking a large share of Nasdaq trading. In May 2001 Reuters sold part of Instinet to the public. A year later Instinet bought Island, an upstart rival that ran its own electronic market.

sections.heading: Anonymous, and After Hours
sections.body: Instinet bet that buyers and sellers could find each other through a screen and save on costs. It offered anonymity, which mattered to large investors who did not want to tip off the market. Its model set the pattern for modern stock markets, and many of today's trading venues follow it. It also let institutions trade outside normal exchange hours.

sections.heading: Absorbed by Nasdaq
sections.body: Instinet priced its IPO at $14.50 a share in May 2001 and listed on Nasdaq. Competition from other electronic networks and falling trading fees squeezed it. In 2005 Nasdaq agreed to buy Instinet Group for about $1.9 billion to get its electronic marketplace. The market Instinet built became part of the exchange it had competed with for years. The brokerage arm went to the private equity firm Silver Lake, and later to Nomura.

cover.artwork: Chicago Stock Exchange Trading Room: Reconstruction at the Art Institute of Chicago

dek: Riverstone made fast routers that let telecom carriers run Ethernet across a city, linking offices and data centers.
lede: Riverstone sold routers to the young telecom carriers, and it went public just as those carriers began to fall. The company was spun out of Cabletron Systems, a networking hardware maker, as Cabletron broke itself into smaller units. Riverstone built routers for metropolitan networks, which linked offices and data centers across a city. In early 2001 carriers still planned huge network buildouts. Riverstone's IPO came that February, as the market for new telecom gear started to fall apart.

sections.heading: Office Ethernet, Citywide
sections.body: Riverstone bet that carriers would use Ethernet, the cheap and familiar technology of office networks, to carry traffic across cities. Its routers combined high speed with controls that let carriers sell different levels of service. The technology was sound. The risk sat with its customers. Its main buyers were the young, competitive carriers of the late 1990s, and many had borrowed heavily to build their networks.

sections.heading: When the Carriers Fell
sections.body: Riverstone priced its IPO at $12 a share in February 2001 and listed on Nasdaq as RSTN. The shares closed the first day at $13.06. Within months, many of its carrier customers cut spending or went bankrupt. The company later faced an accounting investigation and restated its results. In 2006 Riverstone filed for bankruptcy, and Lucent Technologies bought most of its assets.

tagline: Linus Torvalds and a Secret Chip
dek: Transmeta made low-power laptop chips that used software to run Intel-style programs, for longer battery life.
lede: Transmeta worked in near-total secrecy for five years, and its hiring of Linux creator Linus Torvalds only deepened the mystery. In 2000 it revealed the Crusoe processor. The idea was striking: a simple, power-saving chip that used software to act like an Intel processor. It promised thin laptops with long battery life. The company went public in November 2000, one of the last big hardware offerings of the boom.

sections.heading: Code Morphing
sections.body: Transmeta bet that it could beat Intel on power use by moving complexity from hardware into software. Its code morphing layer translated programs as they ran, which let the hardware stay small and cool. Some Japanese laptop makers adopted Crusoe for their thin, light machines. Performance fell short of expectations, and Intel answered with its own power-saving chips. Engineers still study Transmeta's approach.

sections.heading: From Chips to Patents
sections.body: Transmeta priced its IPO at $21 a share in November 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The shares rose sharply on the first day, then fell for years as chip sales stayed small. The company shifted toward licensing its power-saving technology, and it won a large patent settlement from Intel. Its ideas about saving power spread through the wider industry. In 2009 Novafora acquired Transmeta.

cover.artwork: Three Caterpillars, a Moth, and Four Butterflies, from Diversae Insectorum...Figurae

dek: Synplicity made software that turned an engineer's written circuit description into a design for a programmable chip.
lede: Synplicity's stock closed its first day 42 percent above its $8 offering price. More and more chip designers described circuits in code instead of drawing them gate by gate. Synthesis software turned that code into a real design. Synplicity, based in Sunnyvale, built fast synthesis tools for FPGAs, programmable chips that engineers could configure after manufacturing. It went public in October 2000, in a record year for the chip industry, when demand for design tools was high.

sections.heading: A Neutral Tool for FPGAs
sections.body: Synplicity bet that FPGAs would grow from prototyping tools into chips used in real products. Their designers, it figured, would want specialized software. Its tools were quick and worked with chips from many vendors, which gave engineers a neutral choice. The company later added tools for verifying and prototyping larger custom chips. Many hardware engineers came to use its tools in their daily design work.

sections.heading: Folded Into Synopsys
sections.body: Synplicity priced its IPO at $8 a share in October 2000, below the $10 to $12 range it first expected, and listed on Nasdaq as SYNP. The chip downturn of 2001 slowed its growth, and the company kept a loyal base of engineers. In 2008 Synopsys, one of the largest chip design software companies, acquired Synplicity and added its tools to its own line.

dek: CoSine built network gear that let phone carriers sell firewalls and private networks to businesses as a service.
lede: CoSine Communications closed its first day of trading at $63.06, up 174 percent from its $23 offering price. It was one of the most hyped networking startups of the boom. CoSine built large systems that let telecom carriers offer business customers firewalls and private networks from inside the carrier's own network. It went public in September 2000, near the top of the telecom bubble. At the close of that first day, the market valued it at about $6.3 billion.

sections.heading: Security Sold as a Service
sections.body: CoSine bet that carriers would sell security and networking as services. Businesses would then not need to buy and run their own equipment. Its systems let one carrier serve many customers from shared hardware, an idea that looked ahead to later cloud services. Large carriers in the United States and abroad tested its systems. The plan depended on carriers with money to spend on new equipment.

sections.heading: After the Wave Broke
sections.body: CoSine priced its IPO at $23 a share in September 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Goldman Sachs led the offering, which raised about $230 million. Months later the telecom market collapsed, and carriers stopped buying. Revenue never came close to the hopes set at the offering. In 2004 the company wound down its operations. What remained was a shell company that held on to its cash.

cover.artwork: Awa Province: Naruto Whirlpools (Awa, Naruto no fuha), from the series "Famous Places in the Sixty-odd Provinces (Rokujuyoshu meisho zue)"

tagline: Defense Radio Know-How, Sold to Wireless
dek: WJ Communications made radio chips and parts that let wireless base stations and broadband gear carry signals.
lede: WJ Communications carried more than forty years of radio engineering into the wireless boom. It grew out of Watkins-Johnson, a Silicon Valley electronics firm founded in 1957 that built microwave and defense equipment. After a recapitalization led by the private equity firm Fox Paine, the company refocused on radio frequency parts for wireless networks. It went public in August 2000. Phone carriers were racing to build networks, and RF chips were in high demand.

sections.heading: Amplifiers for Base Stations
sections.body: WJ bet that the wireless build-out would need large numbers of high-performance amplifiers and mixers. Its parts sat inside the base stations that carried mobile calls and inside broadband equipment. The company had decades of RF know-how from its parent. Its fortunes depended on the spending cycles of a few big equipment makers. When they ordered, WJ grew. When they stopped, WJ shrank.

sections.heading: A Long Fade
sections.body: WJ priced its IPO at $16 a share in August 2000, the top of its expected range, and listed on Nasdaq as WJCI. Within a year, the telecom slump cut orders sharply. The company shrank, moved to outsourced manufacturing and kept selling RF parts to a narrower market. In 2008 TriQuint Semiconductor acquired WJ Communications and brought its RF know-how into a larger wireless chip company.

cover.theme: a signal tower on a mountain (radio)
cover.artwork: Signal Tower on Elk Mountain, Maryland

tagline: A PC Paid Like a Phone Bill
dek: PeoplePC sold a new home computer and internet access together for one monthly fee.
lede: PeoplePC's biggest moment came when Ford and Delta Air Lines said they would give home computers to their employees through it. Many American households still did not own a computer. PeoplePC, founded in San Francisco in 1999, offered a new PC, internet service and support for one monthly payment, like a phone plan. The employer deals came in 2000. The company went public that August at $10 a share, after it lowered its expected price range.

sections.heading: The Price of Getting Online
sections.body: PeoplePC bet that the cost of a computer was the main barrier to getting online. Spreading that cost into monthly payments would bring in new users. Corporate programs gave it a fast way to reach hundreds of thousands of households. It also sold through partners outside the United States. The model carried heavy hardware costs up front, and it relied on customers staying for years.

sections.heading: Absorbed by EarthLink
sections.body: PeoplePC listed on Nasdaq as PEOP in August 2000. The stock dropped quickly as the market turned and losses grew. The company cut back the hardware offer and focused on low-cost internet access. In 2002 EarthLink acquired PeoplePC. The brand lived on for years as a budget internet service. The idea of a device paid for monthly came back later, in phone plans.

cover.theme: a crowd of people in a park
cover.artwork: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884

dek: Equinix runs the buildings where networks, cloud providers and companies plug their equipment into each other.
lede: Equinix went public with only a handful of buildings open, and those buildings were where the internet's networks met. The internet is many separate networks, and they need neutral places to connect. Jay Adelson and Al Avery founded Equinix in 1998 to build those meeting points. Carriers, content companies and businesses rented space inside and linked their equipment directly. The name nods to equality and exchange. The IPO came in August 2000, a few months after the market peak.

sections.heading: Neutral Ground
sections.body: Equinix bet that neutrality was the product. It was not a carrier itself, so competing networks were willing to meet inside its buildings. Each new customer made a site more valuable to the next, since there were more partners to connect with. Proving the idea took years and large amounts of capital. Its buildings became key points where the internet's networks join.

sections.heading: Through the Bust, Worldwide
sections.body: Equinix priced its IPO at $12 a share in August 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The telecom crash nearly sank it. The company survived through a restructuring and a merger with assets from rivals. It then grew steadily into a worldwide network of data centers, and in 2015 it became a real estate investment trust. It is still public and trades as EQIX.

tagline: Dial-Up for Brazil, Mexico and Argentina
dek: AOL Latin America brought AOL's dial-up internet service to Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Puerto Rico.
lede: America Online had brought tens of millions of Americans online by 2000, and it wanted to repeat the feat in Latin America. It formed a joint venture with the Cisneros Group, a Venezuelan media family, to launch AOL in Brazil, Mexico and Argentina. The venture went public in August 2000, as internet stocks were already falling. It planned to spend heavily on marketing and free trial discs.

sections.heading: Paying What Rivals Gave Free
sections.body: AOL Latin America bet that AOL's easy software and brand would win in markets where few people were online yet. It localized content and spent heavily on promotions. Local rivals offered free internet access, and many users did not want to pay a monthly fee. Phone and broadband companies began bundling their own access. Its parent companies kept funding it for years, hoping for a turnaround.

sections.heading: Lights Out
sections.body: AOL Latin America priced its IPO at $8 a share in August 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Subscribers grew, but the losses were large and constant, and it relied on money from its parents. Its share price sank as free and broadband services spread. In 2005 the company filed for bankruptcy and shut down its service, the end of AOL's dial-up push into Latin America.

dek: WebEx let people meet online from a web browser, sharing the same screen, slides and video.
lede: Showing a presentation to colleagues in another city once meant a plane ticket or a fuzzy phone call. WebEx let people join a meeting in a web browser and see the same screen. Subrah Iyar and Min Zhu founded it in 1995. It ran the service on its own global network and sold it by subscription. WebEx went public in July 2000 as the dot-com market wobbled, and its product kept selling.

sections.heading: Meetings Sold by Subscription
sections.body: WebEx bet that companies would pay to meet online, and that the service should be hosted instead of installed. That made it an early software-as-a-service business. It built its own network to keep meetings fast and reliable. Sales teams were early adopters, giving demos to customers far away. After the September 11 attacks, many businesses cut back on travel, and demand for online meetings grew quickly.

sections.heading: Acquired by the Network
sections.body: WebEx priced its IPO at $14 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. It turned profitable and became the leading name in web conferencing. In 2007 Cisco bought WebEx for about $3.2 billion. Under Cisco, Webex became the core of its collaboration business. Its use surged during the pandemic of 2020, and the product name is still in wide use.

fate: Renamed Raindance; acquired by West Corporation, 2006
dek: Evoke let businesses set up their own conference calls and online meetings, with no operator in the middle.
lede: Evoke Communications went public in July 2000, the same month as its rival WebEx. The two companies made different bets on how meetings would move online. Evoke, based near Boulder, Colorado, sold conference calls and web meetings to businesses, just as both were moving from operators and switchboards to the web. Its customers could set up a call themselves, share slides and invite others without help. The market for online collaboration was still young.

sections.heading: Voice First, Slides Second
sections.body: Evoke bet that conferencing would become a self-service product. Users scheduled and ran their own calls and added web presentations, which cut the cost of each meeting. It sold the service to companies large and small. WebEx focused more on web sharing, while Evoke leaned on voice. That left Evoke's business tied to voice minutes, a market where prices kept falling.

sections.heading: Renamed Raindance, Then Sold
sections.body: Evoke priced its IPO at $8 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as EVOK. It sold 7 million shares. In 2001 it renamed itself Raindance Communications and focused on conferencing for business customers. Raindance stayed public for several more years under its new name. In 2006 West Corporation, a large provider of call services, acquired it. Bigger players with their own networks came to dominate conference calling.

cover.theme: a single voice singing at sunrise

tagline: The Help Desk Turned Bitcoin Miner
dek: Support.com made software and services that fixed computer problems remotely, for companies and then for consumers.
lede: Support.com spent more than two decades fixing other people's computers, then merged with a bitcoin mining company. It started in Redwood City with a simpler idea. When a computer broke, people called a help desk and waited. Support.com built software that let companies find and fix problems automatically or remotely, without a technician on site. It went public in July 2000, as companies spent heavily to support a fast-growing number of PCs.

sections.heading: Tech Support on Autopilot
sections.body: Support.com bet that much of tech support could be automated. Its software sat on users' machines and connected back to a company's help desk. It could check a computer's settings and repair common faults, which cut the number of calls and visits. The company first sold to large corporations, including big technology companies and internet providers. Later it offered remote help to consumers, directly and through partners.

sections.heading: From Help Desk to Bitcoin
sections.body: Support.com priced its IPO at $14 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. For several years it called itself SupportSoft, then returned to the Support.com name. It moved from enterprise software into consumer tech support and outsourced customer service. In 2021 it merged with Greenidge Generation, a bitcoin mining company, and its long run as a tech support company ended.

cover.artwork: Aeneas Rescuing Anchises from Burning Troy

tagline: Thin Servers, Then Other People's Boxes
dek: Network Engines built compact servers and appliances that other tech companies sold under their own brands.
lede: Companies filled data centers with servers as fast as they could in 2000, and every inch of rack space cost money. Network Engines, based outside Boston, built thin, dense servers that packed more computing into each rack. They were built for speed, density and reliability. The company went public in July 2000, when data center space was scarce and the companies building websites seemed to have unlimited budgets.

sections.heading: Boxes Sold Under Other Names
sections.body: Network Engines first bet that web companies would want dense, reliable servers for their growing data centers. When that market fell away, it changed course. It began building ready-to-ship appliances for software makers. They loaded their own programs and sold the boxes under their own names. Security and storage software companies became its main customers, and the shift gave it a steadier business.

sections.heading: A New Engine
sections.body: Network Engines priced its IPO at $17 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell sharply after the dot-com crash, as its web company customers vanished. The appliance business kept the company going for another decade. Through every change, it stayed based outside Boston. In 2012 Unicom Systems acquired Network Engines, and its run as a public company ended.

cover.artwork: Picture of the Steam Engine Railway in Yatsuyama, Tokyo (Tokyo Yatsuyama shita kaigan jokisha tetsudo no zu)

dek: I-many let drug makers track their contracts and rebates, so they stopped losing money to errors.
lede: A drug maker signs thousands of contracts with wholesalers, hospitals, pharmacies and insurers, each with its own rebates and price terms. Tracking all of it on spreadsheets led to errors and lost money. I-many built software to manage those contracts and work out what was owed. It went public in July 2000, while business software was still hot. Investors saw contract software as a fast-growing niche.

sections.heading: Rebates Paid Only Once
sections.body: I-many bet that contract management in health care was complex enough to need its own software. Its products tracked prices, rebates and compliance across many trading partners. Its customers were mainly pharmaceutical and life sciences firms. The tools found money clients were owed and stopped them from paying rebates twice. That made the value easy for finance teams to measure. The company later tried to widen its market to other industries.

sections.heading: Bidding Up a Penny Stock
sections.body: I-many priced its IPO at $9 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as IMNY. Growth slowed after the dot-com crash, and the company posted repeated losses. It kept a loyal base of drug-industry customers. In 2009 the private equity firm LLR Partners agreed to buy it for $0.43 a share. A rival bidder pushed the price up to $0.61, and the deal was valued at about $55 million.

cover.artwork: Flock of Sheep at the Edge of a Wood

dek: Sunrise Telecom made test gear that phone and cable technicians used to find and fix faults in their networks.
lede: Sunrise Telecom's stock jumped 169 percent on its first day of trading in July 2000. The San Jose company made handheld and rack-mounted testers for the technicians who checked telephone and cable lines, found faults and confirmed that service worked. Carriers were building new networks across the country, and test gear was in demand. Telecom equipment stocks were still near their highs.

sections.heading: A Tester for Each Network
sections.body: Sunrise bet that each new network technology would need new tools to test it, from older digital phone lines to DSL, fiber and cable. It built a broad range of instruments and sold them to carriers and equipment makers. Its testers worked in labs and in the field. The work was steady, and it rose and fell with how much carriers chose to spend.

sections.heading: A Long Afternoon
sections.body: Sunrise Telecom priced its IPO at $15 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Carrier spending fell sharply the next year. In 2005 Nasdaq delisted the company after it failed to file reports during an internal investigation into its Korean unit. It moved to the over-the-counter market. In 2013 VeEX bought most of its operating assets, and its products lived on under the new owner.

cover.artwork: View of Mount Fuji at sunrise on New Year's Day

dek: Virage made software that let people search video by the words spoken, the faces seen and the scenes shown.
lede: A news archive might hold thousands of hours of tape with only a few written notes to find anything in it. Virage, based in San Mateo, built software that watched and listened to video. It logged the speech and the scenes, and it made footage searchable like text. Video was spreading online, and it was nearly impossible to search. Virage went public in June 2000, as media companies began moving their archives to the web.

sections.heading: Speech, Faces and Scenes
sections.body: Virage bet that video would become as searchable as documents. Its software combined speech recognition, face recognition and scene detection to build an index of each clip. Broadcasters, government agencies and corporations used it to find footage quickly. It also offered hosted services that let websites publish and search video clips. The market for such tools grew more slowly than the company hoped.

sections.heading: Sold to Autonomy
sections.body: Virage priced its IPO at $11 a share in June 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Like many young software companies, it struggled as tech spending fell after 2001. In 2003 Autonomy, the British search software company, bought Virage and added its video tools to its own products. Later video search services built on the same ideas at a much larger scale.

dek: Click Commerce gave manufacturers one website to work with their dealers and distributors on orders, prices and support.
lede: Click Commerce went public at the peak of the business-to-business internet craze, watched its shares collapse, and then rebuilt itself into a profitable company. The Chicago firm built web software that linked manufacturers with their dealers and distributors for ordering, pricing and support. Many manufacturers sell through such partners, and coordinating that network is hard. Click Commerce listed in June 2000, one of several Chicago tech firms to go public in that period.

sections.heading: One Place for Every Dealer
sections.body: Click Commerce bet that manufacturers would move their partner relationships onto the web. Its software gave dealers a single place to check prices, place orders and get information. Its customers included large manufacturers of equipment and vehicles, and its software ran large parts of their dealer networks. After the dot-com crash, the company bought other software businesses, including tools for research institutions and health care.

sections.heading: Home in Chicago
sections.body: Click Commerce priced its IPO at $10 a share in June 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as CKCM. The shares collapsed after the bubble burst. The company rebuilt itself through acquisitions and a tight focus on profits, and it became steadily profitable. In 2006 Illinois Tool Works, another Chicago-area company, bought Click Commerce. ITW got a profitable software business, and Click Commerce shareholders did better than most of their peers from the class of 2000.

cover.artwork: Chicago River from Rush Street Bridge, No. 188 from the series "Views of Chicago"

tagline: Broadband Down the Old Copper Wires
dek: Centillium made the chips that let phone companies send DSL broadband over the copper lines already in homes.
lede: Phone companies already ran a copper line to every house, and Centillium made chips that turned those lines into broadband. Most homes still reached the internet through a dial-up modem in 2000. Telephone companies wanted to sell faster service without laying new cable, and DSL let them do it. Centillium, based in Fremont, California, designed the chips inside DSL equipment. It went public in May 2000, when the race to wire homes for broadband was at full speed.

sections.heading: Big Orders From Japan
sections.body: Centillium bet that DSL would be the main way households got broadband, and that phone companies would buy huge amounts of equipment to offer it. Its chips went into the gear at the phone company's office and into some home modems. It competed against much larger chip companies for each contract. Its biggest wins came in Japan, where DSL spread quickly and large contracts became a major source of revenue.

sections.heading: Slower Lines
sections.body: Centillium priced its IPO at $19 a share in May 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its bankers had first hoped for $22 to $24. The shares soared at first, then fell as telecom spending dropped and chip prices came down. The company tried new areas such as voice-over-IP and fiber chips. In 2008 TranSwitch acquired Centillium. DSL went on to connect many millions of homes around the world.

cover.theme: electric light arrives (broadband down old wires)

dek: CoolSavings let shoppers pick coupons online and print them at home, paid for by brands and stores.
lede: Americans had clipped coupons from the Sunday paper for generations. CoolSavings, based in Chicago, moved the coupon online. Members signed up, browsed offers from brands and stores by category, and printed coupons at home. Advertisers paid CoolSavings for each shopper who saw or used an offer. The company went public in May 2000, just after internet stocks had begun to fall from their peak.

sections.heading: Every Coupon Has a Name
sections.body: CoolSavings bet that coupons would be a strong lure for online shoppers and a precise tool for advertisers. Members registered, so the company knew who was using each offer. Their profiles let it target offers by place and interest. That made it more valuable to brands than a scattered newspaper insert. The model depended on online advertising budgets, and those budgets shrank sharply after 2000.

sections.heading: Rescued, Renamed, Sold
sections.body: CoolSavings priced its IPO at $7 a share in May 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The dot-com crash cut its advertising revenue. Starting in 2001, loans and investment from the media firm Landmark Communications kept it afloat, and Landmark took control. The company moved into broader online marketing and renamed itself Q Interactive. In 2008 Landmark sold Q Interactive to Intrepid Investments, a merchant bank based in the U.S. Virgin Islands.

dek: HealthStream lets hospitals train and certify their staff online, and keeps the records that prove it.
lede: A nurse on the night shift cannot easily sit in a classroom, and hospitals must train their staff all the time, from new safety rules to required certifications. HealthStream, founded in Nashville in 1990, brought that training online. Its courses and tracking tools let hospitals prove that staff had completed required learning. It went public in April 2000, one of a wave of companies bringing health care onto the internet.

sections.heading: Training Records for Hospitals
sections.body: HealthStream bet that hospitals would move required training onto the web and pay for it by subscription. Its platform delivered courses and kept records of who had completed what. Over time it added tools for scheduling, credentialing and measuring patient experience. It focused on a single industry, which let it build deep relationships with hospital systems. Its customers range from small community hospitals to large health systems.

sections.heading: Still in Nashville
sections.body: HealthStream priced its IPO at $9 a share in April 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell in the dot-com crash. The company kept growing as hospitals adopted online learning, and it expanded into workforce and credentialing software. It is one of the few health care internet companies from 2000 still operating independently. HealthStream is still public, still based in Nashville, and trades as HSTM.

cover.theme: a woman by the lamp (the night shift)

dek: Saba let large organizations plan, deliver and track employee training, then manage performance and talent.
lede: Large companies spent heavily on employee training and had little idea what it achieved. Bobby Yazdani founded Saba in 1997 to change that. His software planned, delivered and tracked learning across an entire workforce. Saba went public in April 2000. E-learning was one of the hottest ideas in business software, and companies were moving training out of classrooms and onto screens.

sections.heading: Learning as a Business Process
sections.body: Saba bet that learning would become a managed business process, tied to each employee's skills and goals. Its learning management system let companies assign courses, track completion and link training to performance. Large corporations and government agencies were early customers, and the list grew to include some of the largest organizations in the world. The company later widened its products to cover hiring, reviews and succession planning.

sections.heading: Restated, Then Sold Twice
sections.body: Saba priced its IPO at $15 a share in April 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The shares fell sharply in the crash, and the company survived and grew. In the early 2010s it faced an accounting scandal and restated years of results. In 2015 Vector Capital took Saba private. In 2020 Cornerstone OnDemand bought it, adding Saba's training and talent software to its own.

cover.artwork: King Solomon Receiving the Queen of Sheba
cover.artist: Master of the Antwerp Adoration Group

tagline: A Real Person Behind the Chat Button
dek: LivePerson makes chat and messaging software so companies can answer customers on their websites and apps.
lede: A shopper with a question on a website in 2000 had to call a phone number or send an email, then wait. LivePerson put a chat button on the page so a real person could answer right away. Robert LoCascio founded the New York company in 1995. Companies paid a monthly fee for each agent. It went public in April 2000, just weeks after the Nasdaq peak, with a product that few companies yet knew they needed.

sections.heading: Several Chats at Once
sections.body: LivePerson bet that live conversation would let websites sell more and serve customers better. Its chat software was hosted, so companies could add it without new servers. Online retailers, banks and telecom companies became major customers. Each agent could handle several chats at once, which saved money for its clients. Later the company moved from website chat to messaging across apps and channels, and added automated assistants.

sections.heading: Below a Dollar, Then Back
sections.body: LivePerson priced its IPO at $8 a share in April 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. In the crash that followed, its shares fell below $1. The company cut costs and held on. It grew steadily through the 2000s and 2010s, as the chat window became a normal part of shopping and banking online. LivePerson is still public and trades as LPSN.

tagline: Selling Band Merch in the Napster Era
dek: ARTISTdirect gave musicians a website to reach fans directly, with news, tour dates and merchandise in one place.
lede: ARTISTdirect went public in March 2000, just as Napster was shaking the music business. Marc Geiger and Don Muller, music industry veterans, founded the Los Angeles company in 1996. They built a network of artist sites and a store for music and merchandise. They also launched a record label with well-known industry figures. Musicians and fans were finding each other online, and the record labels were slow to follow.

sections.heading: A Cut for the Artist
sections.body: ARTISTdirect bet that artists would want a direct line to their fans. A site built around them could earn money from merchandise, advertising and music sales. It gave musicians a share of what their fans spent. Its artist pages offered news, tour dates and merchandise in one place. The idea was early. Fans were moving to free downloads, and online music sales were still years from catching on.

sections.heading: Fading Out
sections.body: ARTISTdirect priced its IPO at $12 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Losses mounted as the dot-com market fell and the label struggled. The company cut back sharply and spent much of the decade searching for a stable business. It never regained the attention it had at its offering. Later platforms made the direct link between artists and fans common.

dek: Websense let employers decide which websites their staff could visit at work, and log the rest.
lede: Offices connected to the internet, and employers soon found staff browsing shopping, sports and worse during work hours. Websense, based in San Diego, built software that sat on a company's network and blocked or logged visits by category. Its database sorted millions of web pages into those categories. Websense went public in March 2000, as businesses rushed to put rules around their new internet connections.

sections.heading: Millions of Pages, Sorted
sections.body: Websense bet that every company with an internet connection would need a way to manage how it was used. It sold subscriptions to its constantly updated list of categorized sites, and that recurring revenue made the business steady. Schools and government agencies became large customers too. Over time Websense moved into broader security, protecting against malware and data leaks as well as unwanted browsing.

sections.heading: From Websense to Forcepoint
sections.body: Websense priced its IPO at $18 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. It was one of the few offerings of that month to grow into a lasting business. In 2013 Thoma Bravo took Websense private for about $906 million. It later combined with Raytheon's cyber business, and the company was renamed Forcepoint. Its filtering and security products carry on under that name.

fate: Taken private by founder Robert Hammond, 2003
dek: PartsBase let airlines and repair shops search one online database for aircraft parts from thousands of suppliers.
lede: Keeping an airplane flying means finding the right part quickly, often from a supplier across the world. Through the 1990s that search ran on phone calls and fax machines. PartsBase, based in Boca Raton, Florida, built a searchable online database of aviation parts listed by thousands of suppliers. It went public in March 2000, at the height of excitement about business-to-business marketplaces.

sections.heading: One Market for Aircraft Parts
sections.body: PartsBase bet that the aviation parts trade would move onto a single shared marketplace. Buyers searched its listings and contacted sellers, and members paid subscription fees for access. Its users included airlines, repair stations and parts dealers around the world. The model fit a niche market where speed and accuracy mattered. It could not match the lofty hopes set by the wider B2B boom.

sections.heading: Back to Private Hands
sections.body: PartsBase priced its IPO at $13 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell steeply as the B2B bubble burst. The company kept serving aviation buyers and sellers. In 2003 founder Robert Hammond took PartsBase private. It was one of the few B2B marketplaces of its era to survive in some form, and it kept operating as a private company.

dek: Caldera sold a business-ready version of Linux, with support and training, to companies running corporate networks.
lede: The company that sold Linux to businesses later sued IBM, claiming Linux used its code. Caldera Systems, based in Orem, Utah, sold a polished Linux distribution aimed at businesses. Linux was the darling of the technology world in 1999. Red Hat and VA Linux had both soared on their first days of trading, and investors wanted more. Caldera went public in March 2000, within days of the Nasdaq peak, and its shares jumped on the first day.

sections.heading: Novell Veterans, Corporate Linux
sections.body: Caldera bet that businesses would pay for a supported, easy-to-install version of Linux, just as they paid for other operating systems. Linux itself was free to download, so Caldera's business rested on what came with it. It offered desktop and server versions, plus training and services. Its founders had worked at Novell before starting the company, and they aimed it squarely at corporate networks.

sections.heading: From Linux to Lawsuits
sections.body: Caldera priced its IPO at $14 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. In 2001 it bought the Unix business of the Santa Cruz Operation, and it later renamed itself The SCO Group. SCO then sued IBM and others, claiming Linux used its Unix code. The Linux world it once sold to became its target. The lawsuits went badly, and SCO filed for bankruptcy in 2007.

dek: ImproveNet matched homeowners with screened contractors and architects for remodels and repairs.
lede: Hiring a contractor has always been a gamble based on word of mouth. ImproveNet, founded in 1996, built an online service that screened contractors and matched them with homeowners planning a project. It checked licenses and references, and contractors paid for the leads. Projects ran from kitchen remodels to new roofs. ImproveNet went public in March 2000, one of many companies promising to bring an old local trade onto the web.

sections.heading: Too Early for the Web
sections.body: ImproveNet bet that homeowners would trust a website to vet contractors, and that contractors would pay for qualified leads. It also offered tools to estimate project costs. Fees from homeowner job leads and contractor bids made up about 55 percent of its 1999 revenue of $2.1 million. The idea was sound, and later companies built large businesses on it. In 2000, too few homeowners were looking for contractors online.

sections.heading: A Remodel of Its Own
sections.body: ImproveNet priced its IPO at $16 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. By then it had lost $42 million since its founding. Its shares fell steeply within months, and the company cut costs to survive. In 2002 it merged with eTechLogix, a private software firm based in Arizona, and new management took over. The combined company moved away from its original consumer focus.

dek: Loudeye turned music and video libraries into digital files and ran online music stores for other companies.
lede: Record labels and broadcasters sat on huge libraries of music and video, and almost none of it was ready for the internet. Loudeye, founded in Seattle in 1997, converted that media into digital formats and hosted it for streaming and download. It went public in March 2000, when streaming media was one of the most talked-about ideas on the web. Six years later, Nokia bought it for about $60 million.

sections.heading: Hire the Specialist
sections.body: Loudeye bet that every media company would need to put its content online, and would rather hire a specialist than build the tools in-house. It digitized vast music catalogs. Later it built a platform that ran online music stores for retailers and mobile carriers. It also bought OD2, a European digital music distributor. Its customers included record labels, radio stations and retailers.

sections.heading: Heard by Nokia
sections.body: Loudeye priced its IPO at $16 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell sharply after the bubble burst, and it changed strategy several times. Its digital music platform caught the eye of Nokia, which was building a music service for its phones. In 2006 Nokia acquired Loudeye for about $60 million and got a ready-made music platform.

cover.artwork: The Seven Trumpets, from The Apocalypse

tagline: Direct Mail Rebuilt for the Web
dek: Digitas used customer data, mail, email and the web so big brands could reach their customers directly.
lede: Digitas started as a direct-mail shop and went public as a digital marketing firm, at $24 a share, well above the $18 to $20 range it first expected. Michael Bronner founded it in Boston in 1980 as Bronner Slosberg Humphrey. By the late 1990s it had reinvented itself, using data to reach customers by mail, email and the web. It went public in March 2000, as big brands scrambled to work out how to market online.

sections.heading: Data Behind Every Letter
sections.body: Digitas bet that marketing would become more personal and measurable. Big companies would need a partner to make sense of their customer data. Digitas combined strategy, data analysis and creative work in one firm. Its work blended the discipline of direct mail with the reach of the web. Its clients included banks, telecom companies and car makers, and they spent heavily on its services.

sections.heading: Into a Global Network
sections.body: Digitas priced its IPO at $24 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as DTAS. Revenue fell in the downturn, and the company recovered as online advertising grew. It bought other agencies, including Modem Media. In 2007 Publicis Groupe acquired Digitas for about $1.3 billion, and it became a core part of Publicis's digital business. The agency still uses the Digitas name today.

dek: Versata let companies build business software by writing down their rules, with less hand-written code.
lede: Versata promised that companies could build software by writing down their business rules, such as how to price an item or approve an order. Its tools then produced the working program. Businesses were rushing to put their operations onto the web, and programmers were scarce. Versata, based in the San Francisco Bay Area, went public in March 2000, at the peak of the market.

sections.heading: Rules Apart From Code
sections.body: Versata bet that business rules could be separated from code, which would let companies build and change applications faster. Its tools ran on popular Java application servers. The approach appealed to large companies with complex logic, and its software handled order processing, pricing and similar tasks. Sales depended on big projects, and those slowed sharply when tech budgets were cut.

sections.heading: Absorbed by Trilogy
sections.body: Versata priced its IPO at $24 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares traded well above the offer price at first, then fell steeply as the market crashed. The company cut staff and shrank for several years. In 2006 Trilogy, the Austin software company, acquired Versata. Under Trilogy, the Versata name became an umbrella for many acquired software products.
